utterances.text: No. They were not autopsied, but there was a criminal investigation examination, a forensic examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you referred to these criminal investigation examination, are you referring to the work that Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic were doing?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I meant by the criminal investigation examination. That's what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So your understanding is that that was a criminal investigation examination; correct? You don't know exactly what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we then move to paragraph 19 of your statement. And it relates to something you just talked about a few minutes ago at transcript reference, draft reference 47, about one woman who gave you details about the deceased, and she told you nothing else. She wasn't -- that woman, she wasn't emotional, didn't tell you anything about how her husband was killed or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So she simply told you -- let me repeat. Was she very calm?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. She engaged in a normal conversation with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So although her husband has just been killed, she was very normal and simply told you that this was her husband and didn't say anything else to you as to what they had done to him or how he had died?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't think the husband was a feature of the evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, we have to look exactly -- we have, as a matter of fact, two identifying persons. Could you please assist the Chamber, perhaps, by - let me just see - we're talking about D2043, at least portions of it, I have, for number 537, I have a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not a matter of critical interest. I can move on. The point was simply that I wanted to confirm that his -- his statement, that nothing -- no more information was given than the identifying details of the deceased. And that's really all I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At paragraph 20 of your statement, I think it relates to something we just talked about in one of my previous questions, when you say: "I think they carried out an on-site investigation, but I am not sure." That's a -- that's your understanding of what they were doing, but you don't know, once again, specifically what they were doing that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: My understanding was that they were carrying out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know that both Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic testified that they did not carry [sic] an on-site investigation in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And they further stated that did not perform any on-site investigations for any of the bodies that they had examined and collected?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Well I don't know exactly what an on-site investigation involves. They had a camera and a video camera with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In paragraph 22 of your statement, you stated Mr. Cermak was in the hamlet of Grubori on that day. Do you know -- do you remember what he was doing there while you were there? Did you see him talk to anyone or do anything?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him. I didn't know who he was. I didn't know that he was Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I didn't ask you if knew who he was. You said he was in the hamlet of Grubori, and I'm asking if you remember what he was doing on that day in the hamlet of Grubori while you were there.

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I saw him seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In paragraph 23 of your statement you say: "Two or three weeks after Operation Storm, we located the bodies of the killed that were not the consequence of Operation Storm." I'm a little confused because Grubori was two or three weeks after Operation Storm. So is that what you were referring to when you said that they were not a consequence of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But then you go on to state that: "In cases like that, the procedure would involve the coroner and the crime police at the scene." And then later on you say: "If an investigative judge needed to be called to the scene where a murder was committed, I do not know whose duty it was to call him ..." To your knowledge, was there a coroner or an investigative judge in Grubori on the 27th of August?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And when you say two or three weeks after Storm that you located bodies of these people in Grubori, that they were not the consequences of Operation Storm, does that mean that all the bodies you had collected before were killed as a result of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If -- if you didn't perform any -- yourself, if you're not involved in any criminal investigation, how can you know whether they were killed in -- as a consequence of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, one could see that the bodies had been in an advanced state of decomposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So are you simply relating -- is it simply a time issue, that if the bodies were collected shortly after Operation Storm, you considered them to have been killed as a consequence of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: But you, in fact, don't know in what circumstances these people were killed whose bodies you were collecting; right?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Serdarevic, I have a few questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You described that -- in your statement, that when you went to Grubori you were in your van, that Mr. Vrticevic was driving in front of you. Did you just follow him, or did you know where you had to go? I mean, who knew the route to Grubori?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, they drove ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you just followed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, coming closer to Grubori, did you notice Mr. Vrticevic still driving his car, or would he board another vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vrticevic and Bilobrk were in the car together with another gentleman I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were they in the car which was used by Mr. Bilobrk and Mr. Vrticevic, or were they in the car that was used that -- or that may have been used by that other person?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I think the car may have belonged to that other person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement we read that you couldn't go up all the way to Grubori. What was approximately the distance where you had to leave your van behind to the village or to the hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall exactly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: 100, 200 metres. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in your statement we read that you had to wait for the crime police to do its job first. You also testified that you talked to a lady. Now, was that after had you done the job, or was that before you did your part of the job, or somewhere in the middle of it?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Before we did our job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You -- your statement is that you had to wait for the crime police to do their job. Was it when you were waiting for the crime police to do their job that you talked to this lady?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you close to the bodies at that moment? Could you see the bodies when you had a conversation with this lady?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did she tell you who the deceased persons were?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: She gave us first and last names of individual persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how did you know what name was linked to what body?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: We didn't write the names down. We merely placed identification numbers on the bodies. The names were only mentioned in the conversation we had with the lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to understand. You talked with the lady. She gave the names. You didn't do anything with that. You said you placed identification numbers on the bodies. When did you get these identification numbers? From whom did you get them and at what moment in time exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: We carried them along whenever we went to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But at one moment or another, the identification number has to be linked to the name of a person. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: We weren't the ones making the link. We were merely placing the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you had the numbers with you. And without knowing to whom or what the name of the person, deceased person was, you just did put that number on it?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you happen to know who, then, linked the name to that body?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you fill in any forms?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said had you to wait for the crime police. Did you have to wait until they have dealt with all of the bodies, or did they call you after they had dealt with one of the bodies, then moved on to the next one, and then would call you for the next one? Or how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: One by one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One by one means once they're done with the one body they would call you or they would fetch you? How did they do that? Did they shout at you, Come over, the job is done, or ... what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: They would call to us. We weren't that far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How far were you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: As I told you, 100 or 200 metres roughly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember who then called you? Was it Mr. Vrticevic? Was it Mr. Bilobrk? Who did it? Who said, Come over and ...

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which of the two. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, then you went to that one body. And did they wait until you were there, or did they go to the next one? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: They would wait for us to get to the body. We would place the number, bag the body, take it to the car, and they would proceed to the next body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would they go with you to the -- to the van, to the car, where you did put the body, or did they not follow you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: They didn't follow us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I understood you well: They did the job on one body; they would call you; you would bag the body and put the number in the bag; then you would bring that body to the van, they did not accompany you. And when you returned, had they started then already with the next body?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this is what happened with all of the bodies, that once they were ready, they would call you; they were there when you bagged the body; then you would bring it to the van, and they would move on to the next one. Is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you well in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I will repeat to you. Whether that was the sequence that followed with all of the bodies: One body -- well, let's say, inspected or whatever done with by the crime police; they would call you; you would bag the body in their presence. Then you would bring the body to the van; they would move on to the next body; and then that same story repeated itself with the second body. That is, once they were done, they would call you; you would come; you would bag the body; put the ID in it; bring it to the van while the crime police would move on to the third body. Is that how it went?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there were others of which you did not know exactly what they were doing there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No. There was nobody by the corpses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I mean in the area of the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There were some others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see any cameras? Did you see any civilians around?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: That was close to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's where they stayed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They didn't follow you into the hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did no one follow you in the hamlet, apart from the persons you had described, that is, Mr. Bilobrk, Mr. Vrticevic, and you and the members of your team; or were there some - whether civilian, whether in uniform - that followed you to the hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they stay at the bridge? Or at what distance were they -- did they stop from the hamlet?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: They stayed by the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is at a distance of approximately how far?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you had left an ID number with the body in the bag, did anyone write down a -- that number, or was it in any way -- was anyone making -- filling any -- filling in any forms or ...

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Vrticevic and Bilobrk were writing down the numbers and so was the team working in -- at the graveyard. They would list all the numbers and then they would place crosses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you put a number next to the body when it was bagged, then they would write down that number?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one line in your statement which was not entirely clear to me. I'll read it to you, and it deals with the beginning of that 27th of August. You said: "On the 27th of August, 1995, just like every morning, we came to Knin first. I did not know from where Mr. Vrticevic was departing Zadar because we telephoned each other and agreed to meet at the coffee bar where we always used to meet." Now, the reference to Zadar is a bit unclear to me. Could you tell us exactly what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: We travelled every day from Knin to Zadar and from Zadar to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you travel to Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon. And in the morning, we would go to Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you were not sure whether Mr. Vrticevic left that morning from Zadar and travelled to Knin or whether he was already in Knin? Is that how I have to understand that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: He had also left from Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the line starts with: "I did not know from where Mr. Vrticevic was departing Zadar." Could you tell me exactly what -- what you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where exactly they were accommodated in Zadar, where they were sleeping in Zadar, at which hotel. That's what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it's clear to me what you didn't know. Now, as far as time is concerned, you went to Strmica that morning, you returned to Knin, left the body that was recovered from Strmica at Knin cemetery, then you travelled to Grubori. Do you remember at what time approximately you left for Grubori from Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time did the whole of the trip to Grubori and the -- the work you had to do there, how much time did that approximately take?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know exactly because we didn't do anything else on that day. We just returned to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You immediately returned from Grubori to Knin. Do you remember how many bodies exactly you recovered in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I think five. And on the way, when we were leaving Plavno for Knin, we found another one in a brook, and we also recovered that body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was just -- you said it was the only thing we did, but you recovered another body on your way back to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I considering -- I considered that the part of the same work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Now, I'm trying to again to -- you said "it was the only thing we did." You travelled to Plavno, then Grubori. How much time did the job take for the five bodies, approximately? Including the time, first crime police, then your part of the job?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps two or three hours, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you. Any further questions, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just one matter of clarification, if I may Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Hedaraly:

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Serdarevic, you just answered the Presiding Judge's question: You said no one followed you from Plavno up to Grubori except for the members of your team and Mr. Vrticevic and Mr. Bilobrk. Earlier in your statement, we discussed what was in your statement about General Cermak being in Grubori and you saw him seated there, didn't know what he was doing. Do you know how Mr. Cermak got to Grubori, if -- if you said no one followed you? I'm just trying to clear up the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Look, I don't know all of the Plavno village. For me, Plavno and Grubori are all one and the same. Mr. Cermak was by the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: So in your statement at paragraph 19 and what we had explored when I asked you questions earlier on where you said that he was -- that you saw him in Grubori but did not know what he were [sic] doing, are you now saying that he was not in the hamlet of Grubori?

utterances.speaker: MILE SERDAREVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he wasn't. He was by the bridge. Whether that is also a part of Grubori or not, that's something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Serdarevic, this concludes your evidence. We'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you. Although, as far as the Chamber is concerned, very unlikely, there's a small chance that we'd need you within the next hour for perhaps two or three more questions. But it's very unlikely. Nevertheless, I would like to instruct you not to speak with anyone yet before we know for sure that we have no further questions for you, not to speak with anyone about your testimony. The Chamber would like to re-call, for a small moment, the previous witness. Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. Serdarevic out of the courtroom. If we don't see you back, Mr. Serdarevic, I already wish you a safe return home and, again, thank you for having answered the questions. Again, the chance that we further need you is minimal. Thank you. Mr. Usher, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you bring the other witness to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know what the -- how long the Chamber is going to go. It's just that it's break time, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. It would be -- it might be - if it takes not more than ten minutes - that we would conclude for the day. We will have a housekeeping session which can unfortunately, not be held today because we -- there are a few new issues. And we -- apart from that, we need someone else to assist us on certain matters who is not in court today. So, unfortunately, we need to have a housekeeping session tomorrow. It will not take very long. So that's not to be done after the break. Therefore, I'm wondering whether we should give it a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's the summary of the statement to be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It will only take three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that. I'm also -- it's a bit of a -- of a gamble. Either we finish in ten minutes from now and then adjourn for the day, or we'd take a break now of 25 minutes and then hopefully finish within ten or 15 minutes. I'm also looking at the booth, whether there's any preference by interpreters and transcribers how to proceed. Could we give it a try? I'm the guilty one. If we do not finish and have to take a break anyhow ... I don't see any gestures that I should not proceed as suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vrticevic, I have a few more questions for you. Further Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I first would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth still binds you. That's the solemn declaration that you've given today. One of the specific points I would like to re-visit is how the sequence was between your work and the work of the civilian protection teams who bagged the bodies and took the bodies to the van. You told us earlier today that you first did the job, photographing, describing, et cetera, for all the bodies, and only then called civilian protection to remove the bodies. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we heard another witness this morning who said, No, that's not how it went. It was they did that job with one of the bodies; then they would call us; and then in their presence we would bag the bodies. We'd then remove the body, take the body to the van, and they, meanwhile, then moved to the second body. Which is a different description of what happened compared to your description. Could you tell us whether this, in any way, refreshes your memory or ...

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat, once again, that, as far as I remember, we processed the bodies there at the site and then we went back while the civilian protection went up there and removed the bodies. That is what I remember, but let me stress that once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Saying that you dealt with all five bodies and then, after that, the bodies were removed. As far as your recollection goes.

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, that's how it went. Maybe it didn't, but I really remember that it should have happened that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did you speak to any of the locals of that hamlet? Did you have conversations with them? Or a conversation.

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I really do not remember. In some cases, the villagers were present; in other cases, they were not. There were many happenings in the 20-odd days that I spent in the field. So, specifically, I do not remember this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you filled in the forms with the ID numbers and the names of the identified bodies. Or -- did you do it, or did Mr. Bilobrk do it, or did you do it together?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I do not remember that specific case, whether it was me or not. But if these pieces of cardboard are there, I could see and then confirm if that was filled in in my handwriting or not. If it wasn't me, then it was my colleague Jozo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could -- are you talking about the lists, or are you talking about the KT-10 forms, which are ...

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the KT-10 forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: D2043, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- could we have that on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the record, D2043.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's got a P on that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yup.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's a very long series. Yes, could we move on. We have, at this moment, 289 before us. Could we move ten pages, expecting that we would then have 299. No, even one further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Page 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... 300. Yes, I do not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One further ... Is that your handwriting? Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: Can I see it. It is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you recognise whose handwriting it is?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the handwriting of Mr. Bilobrk?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't be sure right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I'm first of all asking whether you're familiar with that. And then the next question would be whether you recognise this as his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I can only say that this is not my handwriting. That's not the way I write.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, last question: When you filled in the forms, how did you link the ID number to a name?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: If we had no information, that is, if we didn't know the identity, then we would assign the following number, the ID number. If we had information on identity, we would also give a number and then fill in the form with the -- the first name, last name, and all other information we could gather in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, here, apparently, if you look on the screen, which is one of the Grubori bodies, apparently that person was identified. But you have no recollection as to where that information came from, who the body was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you present when the ID numbers were placed next to the bodies when they were bagged?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. But our job was always the following: We would put the number on the body and then take a photo so that you could see both the face or the upper part of the body and the number on the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we heard evidence which said that once you had done your job, that then the sanitation people would come in, put a number next to the body, and then -- when it was bagged, and that it would then be taken by them and put into the van. Which is, again, a different sequence of -- different to the sequence you describe.

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say it once again. The numbers would go with bags. Now, I can't really remember all those things. I simply can't remember. Can you do whatever you want, but I don't remember. Whether he put those numbers or I put those numbers, I can only say that the numbers were put sequentially, that they were also photographed, all that, and then everything has handed over back in Zadar. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say that when you photographed the bodies the numbers were there, and you do not remember exactly who put the numbers next to the bodies? Did you do it, or did the civilian protection sanitation team put the numbers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA VRTICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anymore. Sometimes we did it, sometimes the civilian protection. As far as I can remember, they would also put the number on the bag itself, and that's how it went to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions of the Bench raised any further matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I don't think it has to be done with the witness, Your Honour, but we have the photographs on the record with the tag on it, so if the Court wanted exhibit numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... no, it's -- I'm aware of that. It's -- Mr. Vrticevic, this then concludes your testimony in this court. We would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and to -- for having answered all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. You are excused. If you wish, you can speak with others again about your testimony. And, Madam Registrar, could you inform the VWS that the other witness ... that the other witness is informed that he is -- not only that he is excused, but also free to speak with whomever he wants about whatever he wants to talk about. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, we have eight minutes left on the tape. I need three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just read a brief summary now of the 92 ter statement of Ivica Vrticevic, who has given evidence this morning. He was a member of the Split-Dalmatia Police Administration in 1995, provided as assistance to the Zadar-Knin Police Administration to carry out tasks of crime scene technician. And he was working on the 27th of August, 1995, in Knin with Officer Bilobrk, and the two of them, that day, went on the following mission. Having been shown a document dated the Knin police log, Exhibit D57, with entries there at one 193 and 198, detailing that the sanitation in the village of Strmica and in the hamlet of Grubori were ordered at 11.00 on the 27th of August, he said he couldn't be in two places at the same time. But he then considered documents that were written at the time, Exhibit D2042, and Exhibit D2043, KTO-10 forms, and as a result of looking at those documents, was able to say that on that day, that he travelled to Strmica and then on to the village of Plavno with officers of the civil protection, as well as Mr. Bilobrk, and he remembered that he saw that day in person, for the first time, Mr. Cermak. And he described him being near the turn for a hamlet of Grubori at the end of an asphalt road and where a dirty road, as it was described, was situated. And he described going into the village of Grubori and the identification of bodies that were considered by him and his colleague on that day and the procedures that were undertaken. And, Your Honour, that is a brief summary of his 92 ter statement, Exhibit D2052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. The Chamber received a table which is a response to its invitation to -- to inform us where the term "postave" is used, rather than "ostave."
